Thanks for the context — good questions. Below are two practical options and the main levers to hit the SLOs. I kept the math high level here; happy to run a focused sizing run once we have the filled SLO-template and an opt-in for a short performance test.

Option A — Optimized (lower cost, moderate ops complexity)
- Model: redwood-7B-quant (4-bit) — good quality/latency tradeoff for summarization & search.
- Quantization: int4 (4-bit) on inference nodes; reduces memory footprint ~2.5–3x vs fp16 and improves throughput.
- Batching: continuous batching window tuned to 10–15ms max to keep p95 under 200ms while achieving effective batch sizes of 32–128 depending on qps.
- Caching: prefix/KV caching for repeated contexts (customer transcripts) — with 20–30% cache hit we cut downstream tokens by similar percent.
- Streaming: enabled for long responses; ensure token flush frequency 50–100ms to keep perceived latency <1s.
- Expected baseline: comfortably supports ~200 qps p95~150–200ms with a modest dedicated pool (example: 6–8 mid-tier GPUs in Dedicated mode).
- Cost: lowest OPEX by leveraging quantized model and aggressive batching/caching; good first step for a POC.

Option B — Conservative (maximize quality & headroom)
- Model: redwood-70B (fp16) or L2-70B equivalent — higher quality for edge cases but >3x memory and cost vs 7B.
- Quantization: optional int8 fp16 mix; requires validation for Q/A quality.
- Batching: smaller windows (5–10ms) to reduce variability; CPU/GPU memory limits will push to larger instance classes.
- Caching: same approach but with more headroom for cache misses.
- Streaming: same flush strategy; might increase compute cost due to longer generation times.
- Expected baseline: will hit targets with fewer engineering tradeoffs but requires ~2–3x the capacity/cost of Option A.

Key cost/performance levers (how they move the needle)
- Quantization (int4): immediate improvements in throughput and instance density. Best first lever for CPU/GPU constrained deployments.
- Continuous batching: best unit-cost lever; tune batch window to your latency budget. If you can accept a 10–15ms batching window, cost per token goes down substantially.
- Prefix/KV caching: for repeated context (support transcripts), cache hit rates directly lower token-generation cost.
- Model variants: routing short queries to smaller, faster variants (e.g., redwood-7B) and heavy contexts to larger models provides the optimal quality/cost frontier.
- Streaming: reduces perceived latency for long responses and lets you optimize compute vs wall-clock by early token flushing.

Sizing caveats & assumptions
- Numbers above assume ~80 tokens average for long responses and 60–80 tokens for short ones; quantized model perf tested on sequences up to 512 tokens.
- Cache hit-rate assumptions are workload-dependent — please provide the SLO-template with percent repeat requests.
- For dedicated capacity pricing we need expected steady-state qps and burst profile (minutes/hour) to recommend autoscaling/burst policies.

Recommended next steps
1) Alex: please fill and return SLO-template.xlsx with token distributions and % repeat contexts.
2) We'll run a 2-hour load test on a small dedicated pool to validate p95 and tuning knobs (requires opt-in).
3) We'll provide a one-page procurement summary (hosted reserved vs private) with ballpark monthly numbers after the test.

I've attached slo-sizing-math.xlsx with a simple model of tokens-per-second, batch efficiency, and cost multipliers you can share with procurement. If useful I can also put together a quick A/B table showing latency vs cost for redwood-7B-quant vs 70B-fp16.
